lessons.title: Case Study: 1 Crore Rupees in a Pune Flat, a Commercial Shop or a REIT

children.text: Sameer Joshi, a 40-year-old engineering manager in Pune, has just sold ESOPs and has ₹1 crore to invest in real estate for about ten years. Three offers are on the table: a 2BHK flat in Baner, a pre-leased shop in Kothrud, and a basket of listed REITs. A broker, a relative and a colleague each insist their option is obviously best. This lesson works through the decision the way a disciplined investor would, using every tool from this course in order: quick screens, net income, tax, ten-year XIRR, scenarios, and fit with Sameer's life. Follow the steps once here, and you will have a template you can reuse for any property decision of your own.

body.text: The best property is not the one with the highest return in one spreadsheet. It is the one that still works in a bad scenario, after tax, and fits the investor's income needs, cash flow and existing exposure.

children.text: The Brief: Who Is Investing

cells: None today; wants income support from about age 50
A child's higher education in around 8 years
Owns the family home in Pune, loan nearly repaid

children.text: The Three Options

cells: About ₹7 lakh (stamp duty, registration, legal, brokerage)
₹55,000 a month; 3-year lock-in; 15% escalation every 3 years
1 vacant month a year; ₹55,000 a year in costs; ₹12,000 property tax
1.5 vacant months a year; ₹33,333 a year in costs; ₹30,000 property tax
Price 6% a year, rent 5% a year
Price 3% a year, rent per lease escalation
Unit price 3% a year, distributions 3% a year

children.text: Step 1: The Five-Minute Screen

body.caption: Quick tests from Chapter 4 (required return assumed at 10%)

cells: Distributions are already net of REIT-level costs

children.text: The screen already sorts the bets. The flat's price assumes strong growth: it needs about 7.3% a year to deliver 10%, above the 6% base case. The shop and the REITs are priced mainly on income and need far less growth. None is ruled out yet, but the flat is clearly the growth-first option.
Step 2: Year-One Income After Tax

body.text: Tax on the flat and shop follows the house property rules from Chapter 4: rent after vacancy and property tax, less 30%, taxed at 31.2%. For the REITs, this case study assumes an effective 20% tax on distributions, reflecting a mix of taxable and lightly taxed components. The real figure depends on each REIT's distribution split and current rules, so treat it as an assumption to test, not a fact.

children.text: Step 3: The Ten-Year Base Case

Now run each option for ten years using XIRR. Each year's net income arrives at year-end, the flat and shop are sold with 1% brokerage, the REIT units are sold with a small brokerage, and long-term capital gains are taxed at 13% on the gain over the ₹1 crore invested.

body.title: Ten-Year Base Case XIRR, Before and After Tax (%)

children.text: Before tax, the flat and shop tie exactly at 7.64%. After tax, the flat pulls ahead, because most of its return is deferred, lower-taxed appreciation, while the shop's rent is taxed every year. The REITs lead in the base case, helped by tiny buying costs and a higher starting yield. But a base case is only one guess about the future.

body.title: Convert to a real return
body.prompt: In the base case, the flat's after-tax XIRR is 6.49%. Assuming inflation averages 5% a year, what is its real after-tax return? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Real return = 1.0649 ÷ 1.05 − 1 = 1.42% a year. After ten years of ownership, tax and inflation, the flat grows Sameer's purchasing power by less than 1.5% a year in the base case.

children.text: Step 4: Stress-Test With Scenarios

markDefs.definition: A deliberately pessimistic scenario used to test how an investment performs if key assumptions go wrong.
A deliberately optimistic scenario used to see how much an investment could earn if things go well.

children.text: In the
bear case
, Pune flat prices grow only 2% a year with 2% rent growth, the shop's price grows 1% a year, and REIT unit prices and distributions each drift down 1% a year as interest rates stay high. In the
bull case
, the flat grows 9% with 6% rent growth, the shop 5%, and REIT prices and distributions 5%.

cells: Real return in the bear case

children.text: The scenarios change the story. The shop has the narrowest range and the best bear case, because its escalations are written into the lease. The flat has the widest range: it is the best bet only if Pune prices boom, and the worst if they stall. The REITs lead in the base and bull cases, but their unit value can end below the original ₹1 crore if prices and payouts fall.

body.title: Which option protects the downside?
body.question: Based on the scenario table, which option gives Sameer the best after-tax outcome if things go badly, and why?
options: The flat, because property always recovers
The shop, because contractual rent escalations keep income rising even when prices barely grow
The REITs, because they have the highest base case return
All three are the same in the bear case
body.explanation: In the bear case, the shop returns 4.75% after tax versus 4.02% for the REITs and 2.98% for the flat. Its 15% step escalations are fixed in the lease, so income keeps rising while the price barely moves. That protection depends on the tenant actually staying, which is the shop's key risk.

children.text: Flat:

₹93 lakh price plus ₹7 lakh buying costs. Rent ₹3,36,000 a year, one vacant month, running costs of ₹55,000 (tenant brokerage, repairs, sinking fund, maintenance while vacant, insurance, paperwork) and ₹12,000 property tax, all growing with rent.
Shop:

₹93 lakh price plus ₹7 lakh costs. Rent ₹6,60,000 a year, rising 15% every three years; vacancy allowance of 1.5 months a year; ₹33,333 a year for insurance, repairs and brokerage averaged over re-letting; ₹30,000 property tax.
REITs:
₹99.9 lakh of units after ₹10,000 brokerage. Distributions start at a 6.3% yield on cost. Effective tax on distributions of 20%. Units sold with 0.1% brokerage.
All options:

income received at each year-end, sale at the end of year 10, long-term capital gains taxed at 13% on gains above ₹1 crore, no loan, surcharge and exemptions ignored, and 5% inflation for real returns.
Step 5: What the Numbers Do Not Capture

cells: Liquidity for education fees in year 8
Must sell the whole flat; months to complete
Must sell the whole shop; thin buyer pool
Sell only the units needed, any trading day
No; assets spread across several cities

children.text: Step 6: The Decision

For Sameer, the REIT basket fits best on balance. It leads in the base and bull cases, provides the most after-tax income from day one, can be sold in parts to pay for education, and does not pile more wealth into Pune on top of the family home. Its weaknesses are real: daily price swings and a bear case where the unit value ends below cost.

The shop is a defensible choice for someone who wants the best bad-year outcome and control over a physical asset, and is confident in the tenant. The flat makes sense mainly for an investor who strongly believes in a Pune price boom, has no liquidity need in the next decade, or may want to live in or gift the flat later. None of those describes Sameer's priorities best.

body.text: Notice what decided the case. Not the highest single return, but the combination of after-tax income, the bear case, liquidity for a known future expense, and concentration in one city. Change any of Sameer's facts, such as a lower tax slab, no education need or no existing Pune home, and a different option could win.

body.title: Name the scenario
body.textWithBlank: A deliberately pessimistic scenario used to test an investment is called the ___ case.
body.explanation: The bear case tests what happens if growth disappoints. A good decision should be survivable in the bear case, not just attractive in the base case.

body.title: Now you decide: Lata's ₹1 crore
body.scenario: Lata Kulkarni, 63, a retired college professor in Pune, has ₹1 crore and faces the same three options. Lata already owns a home, has a pension that covers basic expenses, falls in a much lower tax slab than Sameer, wants about ₹40,000 a month of extra income starting now, and dislikes dealing with tenants. Before tax, the options give year-one monthly income of about ₹21,100 (flat), ₹42,800 (shop) and ₹52,400 (REITs).
body.prompt: Using the six steps from this case study, which option fits Lata best, and what would you check before committing?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Income need: ₹40,000 a month is ₹4.8 lakh a year, a 4.8% yield on ₹1 crore. The flat's roughly ₹21,100 a month cannot meet it. The shop and REITs can.
2. Tax: in a lower slab, tax takes a much smaller bite from rent, so the shop's income advantage over the flat widens after tax, and REIT distribution components matter less.
3. Bear case: Lata cannot wait out a long slump. The shop's contractual escalations give the best bad-year result, but a single vacancy would cut income to zero for months, which is serious for someone relying on it.
4. Effort and liquidity: Lata dislikes dealing with tenants and may face medical costs later. REITs need no management and can be sold in small parts.
5. Concentration: Lata already owns a Pune home, so REITs spread across cities reduce local risk.
6. On balance, a REIT basket likely fits best, possibly combined with safer income sources such as senior citizens' savings schemes and high-quality debt, so that all income does not depend on REIT prices and payouts.
7. Checks: each REIT's occupancy, lease expiry profile, borrowing level, distribution history and component split; how much a 20% fall in unit prices would worry Lata; and the current tax treatment of distributions for someone in Lata's slab, confirmed with a chartered accountant.

body.title: Run your own three-way property comparison
steps: Write down your horizon, income need, tax slab, existing property and any known future expenses.
Screen each option: gross yield, price-to-rent ratio, cap rate and implied growth.
Build year-one net income and tax for each option.
Model ten years of cash flows and calculate pre-tax and after-tax XIRR.
Rerun the model in bear and bull cases, and note the range and the worst outcome.
Convert results to real returns using expected inflation.
Score liquidity, concentration, effort, control and personal use, then decide what fits your life, not just the best base case.

cards.definition: The central, most reasonable set of assumptions for a model.
A pessimistic scenario testing how an investment performs if growth disappoints.
An optimistic scenario showing the upside if things go well.
The gap between bear and bull outcomes; a wider range means more uncertainty.
Liquidity, concentration, effort, control and personal use: the things a return model does not capture.

points: Work through a property decision in order: brief, screen, year-one income, ten-year XIRR, scenarios, and fit.
Sameer's flat and shop tied at 7.64% before tax, but the flat led after tax because appreciation is taxed more lightly and later.
The REITs led in the base and bull cases; the shop gave the best bear case thanks to contractual escalations.
The flat had the widest range of outcomes: excellent if Pune prices boom, worst if they stall.
Liquidity for known expenses and concentration in one city can outweigh a small difference in expected return.
Assumptions, especially tax on REIT distributions, vacancy and growth, drive the answer, so always test them.
Change the investor's facts and a different option can win; the method matters more than any single result.

body.text: This case study is for education only and is not investment or tax advice. The people, properties, REIT yields, growth rates, vacancy, costs and tax assumptions are illustrative, and real outcomes will differ. Tax treatment of rent, capital gains and REIT distributions changes over time, so test your own assumptions and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser and a chartered accountant before making any decision.
